chapter_title: The Basic SELECT Statement and Column Selection
chapter_summary:
Welcome to the core of SQL! The `SELECT` statement is arguably the most frequently used command in database interaction, serving as your primary tool for retrieving data. Think of it as asking your database a question, and the `SELECT` statement is how you phrase that question to get the specific answers you need. At its simplest, you can ask to see all data from a table. For instance, if you have an `employees` table, you can retrieve every piece of information about every employee using `SELECT * FROM employees;`. The asterisk (`*`) is a wildcard character, signifying "all columns." While convenient for quick exploration or small tables, it's often not recommended for production queries or large tables due to potential performance overhead and retrieving unnecessary data.

A more precise and generally preferred approach is to explicitly list the columns you wish to retrieve. This not only makes your query more efficient by only fetching relevant data but also makes your query's intent clearer to anyone reading it. For example, to see just the first name, last name, and email of employees, you would write `SELECT first_name, last_name, email FROM employees;`. Notice that column names are separated by commas. The order in which you list the columns in your `SELECT` statement is the order in which they will appear in your result set, giving you control over the presentation of your data. This explicit selection is crucial for building robust applications and reports, ensuring that your data structure remains consistent even if new columns are added to the underlying table.

To enhance the readability of your query results, especially when column names are cryptic or need to be presented differently in a report, you can use column aliases. An alias gives a temporary, alternative name to a column in the result set without changing the actual column name in the database. You can define an alias using the `AS` keyword, like `SELECT first_name AS "First Name", last_name AS "Last Name" FROM employees;`. If your alias contains spaces or special characters, or if you want it to be case-sensitive, you must enclose it in double quotation marks. Otherwise, the `AS` keyword is optional, and you can simply put the alias after the column name, e.g., `SELECT first_name "First Name" FROM employees;`. However, explicitly using `AS` is often considered good practice for clarity.

Another powerful feature for refining your query results is the `DISTINCT` keyword. Sometimes, your queries might return duplicate rows, particularly when you're selecting only a subset of columns from a table where the full rows are unique but the selected columns might not be. For example, if you want to see all the unique job IDs present in your `employees` table, simply selecting `job_id` might return multiple instances of the same job ID if several employees share that role. To get a list of only the unique job IDs, you would use `SELECT DISTINCT job_id FROM employees;`. The `DISTINCT` keyword applies to all selected columns, meaning it will return unique combinations of the specified columns. If you were to say `SELECT DISTINCT department_id, job_id FROM employees;`, it would return unique pairs of department and job IDs. A common mistake is to think `DISTINCT` applies only to the first column listed; remember, it considers the entire row of selected columns.

Finally, it's worth introducing the `DUAL` table in Oracle. This is a special one-row, one-column table that's incredibly useful for performing calculations, retrieving system values, or testing SQL functions without needing to access a "real" data table. For example, to see the current date and time, you could query `SELECT SYSDATE FROM DUAL;`. Or, to perform a simple arithmetic calculation, you might write `SELECT 10 * 5 AS Result FROM DUAL;`. While it might seem trivial, `DUAL` is a fundamental utility in Oracle SQL for many administrative and testing tasks, and you'll encounter it frequently in examples and real-world scenarios. Always remember to terminate your SQL statements with a semicolon (`;`) in Oracle SQL*Plus or SQL Developer, as it signals the end of a command. Forgetting this is a very common beginner mistake!

screens.title: The Basic SELECT Statement and Column Selection
screens.subtitle: Retrieve data, shape output, remove duplicates, and run quick calculations with DUAL.

narration.text: Welcome. In this chapter you will learn the essential SELECT statement patterns used every day in Oracle S Q L. We will practice retrieving all columns with the wildcard, choosing specific columns to make queries efficient and predictable, and applying column aliases so results are readable for reports. You will also learn how DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from a result set and how the special DUAL table gives you a one-row context for calculations and system functions. These techniques matter because they control performance, clarity, and correctness when you build queries for applications or reports. For example, selecting only the columns you need avoids transferring unnecessary data and keeps result schemas stable when tables change. Using DISTINCT correctly avoids misleading summaries when only some columns are considered. And DUAL is a handy, standardized way to test expressions or fetch system values like the current date. As you move through the lesson, watch the sample employees grid and the code snippets. Notice common beginner mistakes—missing semicolons, misquoted aliases, or assuming DISTINCT applies only to the first column—and try the guided examples to confirm your understanding. At the end, you should be able to write clear SELECT statements, alias columns for presentation, remove duplicates intentionally, and use DUAL for quick calculations. Ready to explore each topic in depth?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: SELECT pulls data. Choose columns explicitly for clarity and performance, use aliases for readable results, use DISTINCT to remove duplicate rows, and use DUAL for single-row calculations or functions.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of these lessons you will be able to write and read basic SELECT statements with confidence. First, you will construct queries that return either every column using the wildcard or a precise set of columns by naming them, which helps both readability and performance. Second, you will apply column aliases to make result headers human-friendly and consistent for reports, using AS or quoted aliases when spaces or case sensitivity is required. Third, you will use the DISTINCT keyword to remove duplicate rows across the selected columns and understand that DISTINCT applies to the entire set of columns, not just the first one. Fourth, you will use the Oracle DUAL table to run simple calculations or fetch system values like the current date without requiring a full table. Each objective emphasizes why it matters in real work: predictable output, smaller data transfer, clearer reports, and safe testing of expressions. You will also learn common mistakes to avoid, such as missing the terminating semicolon, misplacing DISTINCT, or misquoting aliases. These skills give you a stable foundation for building SELECT queries that are correct, efficient, and easy for others to understand.

keyIdea.text: Construct SELECT queries, alias columns, remove duplicates with DISTINCT, and use DUAL for calculations and system queries.

screens.title: How these objectives connect to practice
screens.subtitle: Concrete skills and common pitfalls to watch for

narration.text: These objectives tie directly to everyday tasks you'll do with databases. Constructing precise SELECT statements keeps application layers stable and reduces network and memory load. When you list explicit columns rather than using the wildcard, adding or removing columns in the underlying table won't break your result schema. Using aliases improves report clarity and prevents manual renaming steps after export. With DISTINCT you reduce noisy repetition and prevent overcounting when summarizing categorical values. However, remember that DISTINCT considers the entire selected set of columns, not a single column in isolation. Using the DUAL table is a standard Oracle pattern for testing expressions, returning system values, or computing constants. A common beginner pitfall is forgetting the terminating semicolon in S Q L*Plus or S Q L Developer; another is quoting aliases incorrectly when they include spaces. These small errors cause confusing messages and interrupt workflow. Practice the example queries in a test schema and check results carefully for unexpected duplicates or column name changes. This practical focus will help you move from concept to reliable day-to-day querying.

keyIdea.title: Practical focus
keyIdea.text: These skills reduce errors, stabilize outputs, and make query results readable and efficient in real applications.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Practical Focus

How these objectives connect to practice

Why explicit columns matter

Explicit column lists keep application code stable when tables change. They avoid sending unused data and make the intent of the query clear to teammates.

Aliasing for reports

Aliases let you rename headers for export and reporting without changing the underlying table structure. Use quoted aliases when you need spaces or specific capitalization.

DISTINCT gotchas

DISTINCT removes duplicates across all selected columns. If you see unexpected rows, add more columns to the selection or check grouping logic.

DUAL for quick checks

Use DUAL to evaluate expressions or fetch SYSDATE without relying on table data. It's a lightweight test context used widely in Oracle examples.

screens.title: SELECT * — Wildcard selection
screens.subtitle: When to use and when to avoid the asterisk wildcard

narration.text: Let's define the wildcard usage in SELECT. The asterisk stands for every column in the table and is useful for quick inspection, exploratory querying, or small administrative tasks. For example, SELECT star FROM employees returns all columns and all rows. That is often fine when you are exploring a table schema, but it becomes problematic in production for three reasons. First, performance: fetching every column may transfer large text or binary data you do not need. Second, fragility: if new columns are added to the table, result positions shift, which can break application code that assumes a fixed column order. Third, clarity: other developers reading your code cannot tell which fields the application actually uses. A good rule is to use star for discovery and explicit column lists for code or reports. A common misconception is that SELECT star is harmless if the table is small; in many systems small tables become large with time, or columns with large payloads are added. Practice: run SELECT star for a quick peek, then refine the query to list the columns you actually require. Takeaway: star is a fast inspection tool, not a production pattern. How would you change a broad SELECT star into a focused query for only ID, name, and email?

keyIdea.title: Wildcard use
keyIdea.text: SELECT * retrieves all columns; use it for discovery, not for stable production queries.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › SELECT *
Definition and guidance

The asterisk returns every column in the table. Use it for quick inspection, schema discovery, or debugging, but prefer explicit column lists in production.

Common reasons to avoid *
  • Unnecessary data transfer and slower queries on large columns.
  • Result order or schema can change when new columns are added.
  • It hides which columns the application depends on.
Key Takeaway

Use SELECT * for exploration only. List explicit columns for stable, efficient queries.

Example and quick refactor
-- Quick inspection
SELECT * FROM employees;
-- Refined for production
SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name, email FROM employees;
Misconception

Some assume star will always be fast on small tables. Tables grow and schemas change; choose explicit columns for reliability.

screens.title: Selecting specific columns
screens.subtitle: List the columns you need and control result order

narration.text: Selecting specific columns is the default professional practice. When you list columns by name, the database returns them in the same order you wrote them, which gives you control over the result layout. For example, to surface names and contact info you might write SELECT first_name, last_name, email FROM employees; and the result set will present first name first, last name second, and email third. This ordering matters for reporting and downstream code that expects columns in a particular sequence. Think of it as defining the contract of your query. A simple process to create a focused query starts with identifying the fields you need, then writing them in the desired order, and finally testing the output to confirm columns and types match expectations. A common mistake is to assume the database will reorder columns or that JSON or CSV exports will always label columns — they will use your selected column order. Another risk is leaving out a required identifier like employee_id when fetching display columns; include stable keys when the result will be joined or referenced later. Practice by converting a SELECT star into an explicit list and verifying result schemas. Takeaway question: which columns are essential for your report and which can you safely omit to improve performance?

keyIdea.title: Column selection
keyIdea.text: Explicitly list columns to define output order, reduce data returned, and create a stable query contract for downstream use.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Select Columns

Selecting specific columns

Define exactly which fields you need and the order they should appear.

Process
  1. Identify fields needed for the task or report.
  2. Write the columns in the desired presentation order.
  3. Test the query to confirm column types and names.
  4. Add stable identifiers if results will be referenced or joined.
Example
SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name, email FROM employees;
Why order matters

Result order is the contract between your query and downstream consumers. CSV exports and reporting tools rely on the order you provide.

Misconception

Assuming the database will insert columns in a preferred order is risky. Always specify the order you rely on.

Key Takeaway

Explicit column lists produce predictable, efficient, and maintainable output.

screens.title: Column aliases and presentation
screens.subtitle: Use AS and quoted aliases to label result columns clearly

narration.text: Column aliases give temporary, user-friendly names to columns in your result set without changing the underlying table. They help when original column names are cryptic or when you need space-containing labels in reports. You can assign an alias using AS, for example: SELECT first_name AS "First Name", last_name AS "Last Name" FROM employees; Quoted aliases are required when the alias contains spaces, punctuation, or you want case sensitivity. In Oracle, double quotes preserve the alias verbatim. Another syntax option omits AS and places the alias directly after the column name, but including AS improves clarity. A common misconception is that aliases change the column in the table; they only rename the column in the results of that specific query. Also avoid reusing a column name that conflicts with an existing column unless you intentionally want to hide it in the output. Aliases are particularly useful when you compute expressions, such as SELECT salary * 1.10 AS "Adjusted Salary" FROM employees; where the alias documents the derived value. Practice using quoted aliases for report headers and avoid unnecessary complexity in names. Closing question: which alias style will be most readable for your team, AS or implicit?

keyIdea.title: Alias practice
keyIdea.text: Aliases format result headers for readability; use AS for clarity and double quotes when you need spaces or exact casing.

content.html:
Module 2›Chapter 2.1›Aliases

Column aliases and presentation

Alias styles compared
Using AS with quotes: SELECT first_name AS "First Name" FROM employees;
Using AS without quotes: SELECT first_name AS FirstName FROM employees;
Implicit alias: SELECT first_name "First Name" FROM employees;
When to quote

Quote the alias when you need spaces or specific capitalization in the output header. Unquoted identifiers are folded to upper case in Oracle unless quoted.

Example with expression
SELECT salary * 1.10 AS "Adjusted Salary" FROM employees;
Misconception: aliases change the table. They do not — aliases only label the column in the query results.

screens.title: The DISTINCT keyword
screens.subtitle: Eliminate duplicate rows from the selected column set

narration.text: DISTINCT is a modifier placed after SELECT that removes duplicate rows from the result set across all selected columns. When you write SELECT DISTINCT job_id FROM employees; the database returns only unique job IDs that exist in the table. Crucially, DISTINCT considers combinations: SELECT DISTINCT department_id, job_id FROM employees; returns unique department and job ID pairs. A common misunderstanding is to think DISTINCT applies only to the first column or that it behaves like GROUP BY — DISTINCT simply filters out duplicated result rows. In practice, use DISTINCT when you need a list of unique values or unique combinations, like finding all departments represented in a table. Remember that DISTINCT may incur additional work for the database because it must compare rows to remove duplicates; if you only need counts or aggregations, GROUP BY or analytic functions may be more appropriate. Example: if three employees share the same job_id, selecting job_id without DISTINCT will list that job_id three times; with DISTINCT it appears once. Takeaway: use DISTINCT intentionally to produce unique rows and be aware of its scope being the full selected column list. How would you verify that DISTINCT returned all unique combinations you expected?

keyIdea.title: DISTINCT usage
keyIdea.text: DISTINCT returns unique rows across the set of selected columns; it filters duplicate combinations, not individual columns independently.

content.html:
Module 2›Chapter 2.1›DISTINCT

The DISTINCT keyword

Definition

DISTINCT removes duplicate rows in the result, considering the entire set of selected columns as the unit for uniqueness.

Example
SELECT DISTINCT job_id FROM employees;
Misconception: DISTINCT applies only to the first column listed. It does not; it applies to the whole selected row.
Multiple columns

SELECT DISTINCT department_id, job_id FROM employees; gives unique pairs. If you need unique departments alone, select DISTINCT department_id.

Performance note

DISTINCT can require sorting or hashing to remove duplicates. Use it when the semantics require uniqueness; otherwise consider aggregation or indexes to support performance.

Key Takeaway

DISTINCT filters duplicate result rows across the selected columns; use it purposefully and verify results.

screens.title: Practical examples: SELECT, aliases, and DISTINCT
screens.subtitle: Live-style code snippets you can run in SQL Developer or SQL*Plus

narration.text: Now let's walk through concrete code examples you can execute in S Q L Developer or S Q L*Plus. Start by inspecting the table: run a quick SELECT star FROM employees; to see available fields. Then narrow the result: SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name, salary FROM employees; lists only the needed columns. To make headers readable in a report, add aliases: SELECT first_name AS "Employee First Name", last_name AS "Employee Last Name" FROM employees; Notice the double quotes around aliases that include spaces. Next, use DISTINCT to find unique department IDs: SELECT DISTINCT department_id FROM employees; and to find unique department and job combinations: SELECT DISTINCT department_id, job_id FROM employees ORDER BY department_id, job_id; I recommend adding ORDER BY to get consistent output when reviewing results. A common beginner error is forgetting the trailing semicolon in S Q L*Plus or S Q L Developer; that semicolon marks the end of the statement in Oracle tools. Another frequent mistake is misplacing quotes around aliases, which leads to identifier or syntax errors. Practice these snippets and check the result set headers and row counts to ensure they match expectations. Closing thought: run the examples and then change one column in the SELECT list to see how the result changes, reinforcing how selection shapes output.

keyIdea.title: Run-ready code
keyIdea.text: Try these example queries in a safe environment to see how SELECT, aliases, and DISTINCT affect results and headers.

content.html:
Module 2›Chapter 2.1›Code Walkthrough

Practical examples: SELECT, aliases, and DISTINCT

-- 1. Inspect table
SELECT * FROM employees;
-- 2. Focused columns
SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name, salary FROM employees;
-- 3. Aliases
SELECT first_name AS "Employee First Name", last_name AS "Employee Last Name" FROM employees;
-- 4. DISTINCT examples
SELECT DISTINCT department_id FROM employees;
SELECT DISTINCT department_id, job_id FROM employees ORDER BY department_id, job_id;
Execution guidance
  • Always end statements with a semicolon in Oracle tools.
  • Use ORDER BY with DISTINCT when you want repeatable output ordering.
  • Verify aliases appear exactly as you expect in exports by using quotes when needed.
Common errors
Missing semicolon causes the client to wait for the statement terminator.
Incorrect alias quoting leads to syntax or unexpected identifier names.
Try this

Run the four examples in a test schema, then remove one column from the SELECT list to see how results and duplicates change.

screens.title: The FROM clause and statement termination
screens.subtitle: FROM specifies source tables and the semicolon ends a statement

narration.text: The FROM clause tells the database which table or tables supply rows to your SELECT. Without FROM, SELECT can still be used with DUAL for expressions, but when you want real data you must name the table: SELECT first_name, last_name FROM employees; In Oracle S Q L*Plus and S Q L Developer, statements must be terminated with a semicolon; this marks the end of the S Q L command to the client. Forgetting the semicolon is a common beginner error that leads the client to await further input or raise a syntax message. Another subtle point: FROM can reference views or subqueries, not only base tables. When selecting from multiple tables you will later add JOIN clauses, but for this chapter focus on single-table selection. A common misconception is that FROM defines columns — it does not; it only defines the row source. Columns are resolved against the named table(s). When testing queries, confirm your FROM clause references the expected table and that your user has permission to read it. Closing question: if you omit the semicolon in S Q L Developer, what behavior do you observe and how does adding it change execution?

keyIdea.title: FROM and semicolon
keyIdea.text: FROM specifies the source table(s) for rows; in Oracle clients a trailing semicolon terminates the SQL statement for execution.

content.html:
Module 2›Chapter 2.1›FROM & Semicolon
FROM clause

Specify the source table or view. Columns in the SELECT are resolved against this source. For example: SELECT first_name, last_name FROM employees;

Permissions note

Ensure your user has SELECT privileges on the referenced table; otherwise queries will fail with permission errors.

Statement termination

In Oracle SQL tools, end statements with a semicolon. Missing the semicolon makes the client wait or produce syntax messages.

SELECT first_name FROM employees -- missing semicolon SELECT first_name FROM employees; -- correct
Common mistake

Forgetting the semicolon interrupts execution; always end statements in Oracle clients.

screens.title: Using the DUAL table
screens.subtitle: Single-row context for calculations and system functions

narration.text: Oracle's DUAL table is a special one-row, one-column table used for evaluating expressions and returning system values without needing a real data table. It is convenient when you want to compute a value or check a function. For example, to get the current database date you might run SELECT SYSDATE FROM DUAL; and to calculate a numeric expression use SELECT (150 * 3) + 25 AS "Calculation Result" FROM DUAL; DUAL saves you from creating throwaway tables for simple tests. Remember that queries selecting expressions without a FROM clause may be allowed in some databases, but in Oracle the standard pattern is to select FROM DUAL. A common misconception is that DUAL is for production queries — it is intended for expressions, diagnostics, and small administrative checks, not for returning business data. DUAL always returns exactly one row, so be careful when embedding it in larger queries; its one-row behavior is the reason it is useful for calculations and scalar function checks. Try using DUAL when you want to test a formula or check a function's output before integrating it into a larger SELECT from a table.

keyIdea.title: DUAL table
keyIdea.text: DUAL is a one-row utility table for calculations and system values in Oracle; use it to test expressions or fetch SYSDATE.

content.html:
Module 2›Chapter 2.1›DUAL
What is DUAL?

DUAL is a built-in single-row table used to select expressions, constants, or system functions in Oracle, without querying application data.

Examples
SELECT SYSDATE FROM DUAL; SELECT (150 * 3) + 25 AS "Calculation Result" FROM DUAL;
Why use it

It provides a predictable single-row context for evaluating expressions and testing functions before integrating them into larger queries.

Misconception: DUAL is for business data. It isn't. It's a utility for testing and evaluation, not for storing transactional records.
Key Takeaway

Use DUAL to evaluate expressions and fetch system values in Oracle without referencing a real table.

screens.title: DISTINCT vs GROUP BY
screens.subtitle: When to use DISTINCT and when to prefer GROUP BY

narration.text: DISTINCT and GROUP BY can both produce unique combinations, but they serve different purposes. DISTINCT filters duplicate result rows across selected columns and returns the unique set. GROUP BY, by contrast, groups rows to allow aggregation like counts or sums per group. For example, SELECT DISTINCT department_id FROM employees; returns unique department IDs. To count employees per department you would use GROUP BY: SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id; Here, GROUP BY creates buckets and lets you compute aggregates per bucket. A common misconception is to use DISTINCT when an aggregate is required; DISTINCT cannot compute totals or averages. Another distinction: GROUP BY can be more flexible when combined with aggregate functions and HAVING clauses for filtering groups. Use DISTINCT when you only need the set of unique rows without aggregation, and use GROUP BY when you need summarized metrics per group. Example: to get unique department and job pairs use DISTINCT; to count how many employees share each job use GROUP BY job_id with COUNT. Takeaway: pick DISTINCT for deduplication and GROUP BY for aggregation and summaries.

keyIdea.title: Choose correctly
keyIdea.text: Use DISTINCT to deduplicate rows; use GROUP BY when you need aggregation or group-level filtering.

content.html:
Module 2›Chapter 2.1›DISTINCT vs GROUP BY
DISTINCT

Returns unique rows for the selected columns. Use when you need just the distinct set.

SELECT DISTINCT department_id FROM employees;
GROUP BY

Groups rows to compute aggregates like counts, sums, averages per group.

SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id;
Misconception: using DISTINCT to emulate GROUP BY totals won't produce aggregates. Use the correct tool for the goal.
Key Takeaway

DISTINCT deduplicates; GROUP BY summarizes. Choose based on whether you need aggregates.

screens.title: Hands-on activity walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step tasks using the employees table

narration.text: Let's walk through the hands-on scenario step-by-step so you can apply what you've learned. Begin by connecting to your Oracle database and opening a S Q L worksheet. Step one: retrieve all columns to inspect the table with SELECT * FROM employees; This gives you the column names and data types. Step two: craft a focused query to return employee_id, first_name, last_name, salary — write SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name, salary FROM employees; Step three: alias first and last names for a report using SELECT first_name AS "Employee First Name", last_name AS "Employee Last Name" FROM employees; Step four: find unique department IDs using SELECT DISTINCT department_id FROM employees; Step five: find unique department and job pairs with SELECT DISTINCT department_id, job_id FROM employees ORDER BY department_id, job_id; Finally, use DUAL to compute a value with SELECT (150 * 3) + 25 AS "Calculation Result" FROM DUAL; After each query, verify columns, record counts, and headers. Watch for missing semicolons and alias quoting errors while you practice. This process builds muscle memory: inspect, refine columns, label for presentation, deduplicate when required, and test expressions in DUAL. Which step felt least familiar and why?

keyIdea.title: Practice steps
keyIdea.text: Inspect with SELECT *, refine columns, apply aliases, use DISTINCT for unique values, and use DUAL for calculations.

screens.title: Common syntax and logic errors
screens.subtitle: Fix missing semicolons, alias quoting, and DISTINCT misuses

narration.text: Beginners commonly encounter a few recurring errors when writing SELECT statements. First, forgetting the terminating semicolon in Oracle clients causes the client to wait for more input or report an incomplete statement. Always end statements with a semicolon when using S Q L*Plus or S Q L Developer. Second, alias quoting mistakes: when you use spaces or special characters in an alias and forget the double quotes, Oracle treats the alias as an unquoted identifier and folds it to upper case or raises an error. Use double quotes around aliases that contain spaces: SELECT first_name AS "First Name" FROM employees; Third, misuse of DISTINCT: some assume DISTINCT affects only one column or that it deduplicates entire table rows regardless of selected columns. In reality, DISTINCT applies to the selected column set. If you need aggregated counts or group-level summaries, use GROUP BY with aggregate functions. Fourth, relying on SELECT * in application code leads to unexpected schema changes when columns are added. Replace star with explicit columns in production code. Finally, omitting stable keys like employee_id in result sets can make later joins fragile. Check your queries for these issues before promoting them to shared scripts. Which of these errors have you seen most often in your work?

keyIdea.title: Errors to watch
keyIdea.text: Common errors: missing semicolons, wrong alias quoting, incorrect DISTINCT assumptions, using SELECT * in production, and omitting stable keys.

content.html:
Module 2›Chapter 2.1›Common Mistakes
Missing semicolon

Without the semicolon, Oracle clients may prompt for more input or return an error. Always terminate statements.

Alias quoting errors

Use double quotes for aliases containing spaces or special characters to ensure headers appear as intended.

DISTINCT misunderstandings

DISTINCT applies to the full selected column set. If you want summaries or totals, use GROUP BY and aggregates instead.

Using SELECT *

Don't rely on SELECT * in production: it creates fragile contracts and can fetch unnecessary data.

Pro tip

Run queries in a test schema first. Inspect headers, row counts, and types to catch syntax and logic errors early.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize three concise ideas to carry forward. First, SELECT retrieves data: use SELECT star for exploration but prefer explicit column lists in production to maintain performance and a stable result schema. Second, aliases and DISTINCT shape your output: aliases label columns for readability and DISTINCT removes duplicate rows across the selected columns. Use quoted aliases when you need spaces or exact casing. Third, DUAL is your lightweight test table in Oracle, returning one row so you can evaluate expressions or fetch system values like the current date. Together these concepts let you write clearer, faster, and more predictable queries. Keep practicing the hands-on examples: inspect with SELECT star, refine columns, alias for presentation, deduplicate with DISTINCT when needed, and use DUAL for quick checks. keyIdea.text: SELECT intentionally, alias for clarity, use DISTINCT for uniqueness, and use DUAL for expressions and system values.

Module 2›Chapter 2.1›Key Concepts
SELECT and *

Wildcard returns all columns for quick inspection; prefer explicit lists for production.

Aliases

Use AS and quoted aliases for readable result headers, especially in reports.

DISTINCT & DUAL

DISTINCT removes duplicate rows across selected columns; DUAL returns one row for expressions and system values.

Takeaway: write explicit, readable SELECT statements and test expressions using DUAL. That practice prevents surprises and keeps your queries efficient.

screens.title: Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three short reminders for daily use

narration.text: Use this quick reference as a memory aid. First, list explicit columns whenever the query will be used by applications or reports, because it stabilizes schemas and reduces unnecessary data. Second, prefer AS with quoted aliases when you need readable or spaced headers; quoted aliases preserve the exact label. Third, use DISTINCT only when you need unique rows across the selected columns and use DUAL for single-row calculations or to get system values. Keep these three reminders in mind when you open your S Q L worksheet and they will reduce errors and speed debugging. Which of these reminders will you pin to your workspace as a cheat-sheet?
